s: malicious enjoyment derived from observing someone else's misfortune; schadenfreude; gloating
Man empfieng ihn mit einem Gesicht, worauf Schadenfreude und Entrüstung mit schrecklichen Farben sich mahlten, seine Verwunderung dauerte nicht lang: […].
Jedoch ist Neid zu fühlen, menschlich; Schadenfreude zu genießen, teuflisch.
However, to feel envy is human; to relish in schadenfreude, diabolic.
Scheldt (a river in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, emptying into the North Sea)
He is driving a fast car.
schnell.et: From Middle High German snël, from Old High German snël (“nimble, brave, quick, lively”), from Proto-West Germanic *snel, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, bold, quick”). Cognate with Dutch snel, Low German snell, English snell. More at snell.

s: again; quick; used after a question to imply that one ought to know the answer
schnell.et: From Middle High German snël, from Old High German snël (“nimble, brave, quick, lively”), from Proto-West Germanic *snel, from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, bold, quick”). Cognate with Dutch snel, Low German snell, English snell. More at snell.

Schaf.et:
From Middle High German schâf, from Old High German scāf.
Akin to Bavarian Schåf, Luxembourgish Schof, Hunsrik Schof, German Low German Schaap, Dutch schaap, Afrikaans skaap, English sheep, and West Frisian skiep. See sheep for more.

s: destiny, fate (irresistible power that predetermines events)
life story; the general conditions and main developments of a person's life; more often than in English used without any notion of predetermination
Das Buch beschreibt die Schicksale von zehn Frauen aus verschiedenen Gesellschaftsschichten im frühen 20. Jahrhundert.
The book portrays the life stories of ten women from different social classes in the early 20th century.
Schicksal.et: 17th century, from schicken + -sal, after now archaic Dutch schiksel (16th c.).

s: viburnum (any shrub of the genus Viburnum, in particular the guelder rose, Viburnum opulus)
Nowhere is there a land more beautiful than ours at this time [or in this age]...
Der Sonnenuntergang am Strand war wirklich schön.
The sunset on the beach was really beautiful.
Am liebsten entfloh sie dem allem in den großen Garten. Da verbrachte sie ihre schönsten Stunden.
She liked best to escape from all of that into the big garden. There she spent her most pleasant hours.
schön.et: Inherited from Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz.
Inherited from Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōni, from Proto-West Germanic *skaunī, from Proto-Germanic *skauniz.

s: Bei aller Ernsthaftigkeit und Respekt dürfen natürlich Witz und Wiener Schmäh nicht fehlen – denn schließlich kann man nur mit Humor die schlimmsten Dinge im Leben bewältigen.
For all its seriousness and respect, wit and Viennese charm must not be forgotten — after all, humour is the only way to cope with life’s greatest challenges.

Schlucht.et:
There are two etymological paths whose accuracy and possible interrelation are not conclusively established.
* Schlucht is most readily explained as a Middle Low German form of the archaic High German equivalent Schluft, with the Low German development of -ft-…

s: Der Schnee schmilzt wegen des heißen Wetters.
The snow is melting because of the hot weather.
Schnee.et: From Middle High German snê, from Old High German snēo, from Proto-West Germanic *snaiw.

s: physical pain, ache (practically, as a sensation)
Das waren die schlimmsten Schmerzen, die ich je erlebt habe.
That was the worst pain I have ever felt.
physical pain (theoretically, as a bodily mechanism or function)
Schmerz ist ein Alarmsignal des Körpers.
Pain is an emergency signal of the body.
Man lebt weiter, aber der Schmerz bleibt.
One lives on, but the pain remains.
Schmerz.et: From Middle High German smerze m or f, from Old High German smerza f, smerzo m, from Proto-West Germanic *smertan. Cognate with English smart, Dutch smart.

s: Hab ich vor dem Menschen ein heimlich Grauen, / Und halt ihn für einen Schelm dazu! / Gott verzeih mir's, wenn ich ihm unrecht tu!
Das große Wort führt ein Junge, Lasso (Emil Vandersee), ein Schelm in gestreiften Hosen.
Schelm.et: From Middle High German schelme (“pest, plague; those who have fallen in battle”), Old High German scalmo (“plague”), from Proto-West Germanic *skalmjan, umlauted derivation from *skalman (“plague, epidemic, corpse”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Pro…

s: a pity, a shame; bummer; unfortunate; disappointing
Meine neuen Schuhe sind zu schade, um damit durch den Wald zu laufen.
My new shoes are too good to wear them for a walk through the forest.
Ich bin mir fürs Kloputzen nicht zu schade.
I don’t consider myself too good to clean the loo.
schade.et: From predicative use of Schade, the obsolete nominative singular of Schaden (“damage”). The sense “too good” from a conditional construction es wäre zu schade … (“it would be a pity to …”), but now usually construed with an indicative verb.

s: Schaffhausen (the capital city of Schaffhausen canton, Switzerland)

On their grave a lime-tree grows, / Where birds and evening breezes whistle, / And on the turf beneath it sit / The miller-lad and his love.
Schatz.et:
From Middle High German schaz, schatz, from Old High German skaz, scaz, from Proto-West Germanic *skatt (“cattle, treasure”).

Schlüssel.et:
From Middle High German slüȥȥel, from Old High German sluȥȥil, from Proto-West Germanic *slutil, which is derived from *sleutan (“to close”), from which also modern German schließen.
Cognate with Dutch sleutel and English slot.

s: black, reflecting little or no light
black, having a high amount of melanin in an organ, e.g. the skin
of the CDU or CSU (large center-right Christian Democratic parties, whose associated colour is black)
of the ÖVP (conservative party, whose associated colour is black)
not having won any trick (or only tricks with zero points)
Goth (of Goth music or culture, called schwarze Szene (“black scene”) in German)
schwarz.et:
From Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”).
Compare Dutch zwart, English swart and swarthy, West Frisian swart, Danish sort, …

s: having effeminate or flamboyant qualities; fruity, queer, swishy
Haupts Definition seiner Geschlechtsidentität lautet: "Klar, man hat sich schwul zu verhalten." Auf eine noch kürzere Formel gebracht: Schwul sein, ohne Schwuchtel zu sein.
Haupt's definition of his gender identity is: "Sure, you have to act gay." Put even more succinctly: Being gay without being a sissy.
schwul.et:
Borrowed from Middle Low German swōl, swūl (“sultry, hot and humid”) (17th century), adopted into Standard German as schwül in the 18th century, ultimately from the root of schwelen (“to smoulder”).
The older form without umlaut appears in Berlin dialect in th…

s: Willy Brandt war ein Vaterlandsverräter, linke Intellektuelle waren Schmeißfliegen und die Grünen Terroristenfreunde. Der Wahlsieg heiligte die Mittel.
Schmeißfliege.et: From schmeißen (“to defecate”, literally “to throw”) + Fliege (“fly”).

Schweinefleisch.et: From Schwein (“pig”) + Fleisch (“meat”). Compare Silesian East Central German Schweinefleesch, English swineflesh (“pig-meat, pork”).

s: Das Katana war ein weit verbreitetes Schwert in Japan.
The katana was a very common sword in Japan.
dorsal fin (of certain kinds of whales)

schmuck.et: Borrowed from Middle Low German smuk (“supple, bendsome, pleasing, beautiful, petite, cute”) (compare Middle Low German smuk (“ornament, jewellery”)), from Old Saxon *smuk, *smukk, from Proto-Germanic *smukkaz (“flexible, bendsome, easy”).

Schwein.et:
From Middle High German swīn, from Old High German swīn (akin to Old Saxon swīn), from Proto-West Germanic *swīn.
Compare Low German Swin, Swien, Schwien (Schweyn), Dutch zwijn, English swine, Danish svin (also comparable to Latin suīnus and to Polish świnia).

s: to shout; to yell; to cry; to scream; to howl

s: Und sie ging gebückt, als trage sie eine schwere Last, […]
And she walked bowed as if she carried a heavy load, […]
Seine Lider waren wie Blei so schwer, die Zunge gehorchte dem einfachen Gedanken nicht recht, als er aus Artigkeit mit der Engländerin zu plaudern versuchte; […].
His eyelids were heavy as lead; his tongue would not shape his simple thoughts when out of politeness he tried to talk to the Englishwoman.
heavy (doing the specified activity more intensely)
„Es ist überhaupt keine Zeit“, sagte Hans Castorp mit schwerer Zunge.
“You can't call it time,” quoth Hans Castorp thick-tongued.
[Director.] So könnt ihr euch vom Ziele nie verirren, / Sucht nur die Menschen zu verwirren, / Sie zu befriedigen ist schwer – –
Thus shall you hit the mark of gain and glory / Seek to confound your auditory! / To satisfy them is a task.—
schwer.et: From Middle High German swær, from Old High German swār, from Proto-West Germanic *swār, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy, grave, serious”).

s: snake, a treacherous person (especially a woman)
Schlange.et: From Middle High German slange, from Old High German slango, from Proto-Germanic *slangô. Cognate with German Low German Slang (“snake”), Dutch slang (“snake”), West Frisian slang (“snake”). Compare also Albanian shlligë (“adder”).

s: a municipality of Lippe district, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany

Schiedsrichter.et: The second part is akin to Richter; the first part is akin to Middle High German schideman and to Old High German scidōn (“to separate, distinguish, decide”).

Schuh.et:
From Middle High German schuo, levelled variant of schuoch (inflected schuo(h)-), from Old High German scuoh (“shoe”), from Proto-West Germanic *skōh. More at shoe.
Cognate with Luxembourgish Schong, Dutch schoen, Low German Schoh, West Frisian skoech, English…

s: Denn wir wissen ganz bestimmt / Dass wir beide Schatten sind
For we know with certainty / That we are both shadows
Schatten.et: From Middle High German schate, schatwe, schatewe, schetewe, from Old High German scato, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu; akin to Old Saxon skado, Dutch schaduw, English shadow and shade. More at shadow.

Schema.et: Borrowed from Latin schema. Not related to Schemen.

s: agent noun of schleppen: criminal individual who organises human trafficking or people smuggling
agent noun of schleppen: tugboat (boat used to pull barges or to help maneuver larger vessels)
agent noun of schleppen: platter lift (system for pulling skiers uphill, along the surface of the slope)

Schmuck.et: Borrowed from German Low German smuk, related to schmücken (“to decorate”); see there for more. Somewhat displaced Zier (“ornament”).

s: a cocktail with equal parts beer and cola
Schmutz.et: From Middle High German smuz. Cognate with Middle English bismitten (“to stain, soil”), Dutch smet (“spot, dirt”), English smut. Likely related to schmuddeln (“to become dirty”); see there for more.

s: the cochlea in the inner ear
scroll (the carved wooden spiral at the end of a stringed instrument's fingerboard)
pastry in the form of a snail
a stylized charge consisting of a tapering spiral inward from the edge to the centre of the shield, somewhat resembling the spiral on a snail's shell or a gurges
1924 (RORDORF) Zürich h f K. 72 : 122. Stehender geharnischter Ritter mit Lanze, Schwert und erhobenem Wappenschild mit Schnecke. Visir geöffnet. Helmzierde mit fünf Pfauenfedern besteckt.
Schnecke.et: From Middle High German snëcke, from Old High German sneggo, snecco, from Proto-Germanic *sneggô.

s: shva (one of the nikud (Hebrew vowel signs))
Das Schwa wird bald wie ein schwaches e ausgesprochen, und heisst dann Schwa mobile, bald wird es gar nicht gesprochen, und heisst Schwa quiescens.
Schwa.et: Learned borrowing from Hebrew שווא / שְׁוָא (š’wā, “nought”).

Schwarz.et: From the adjective schwarz, from Middle High German swarz, from Old High German swarz, from Proto-West Germanic *swart, from Proto-Germanic *swartaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swerd- (“dirty, dark, black”). Compare German schwarz, Dutch zwart, English swart.

Wenn Schafe nicht geschoren werden, können sie sich vor lauter Wolle nicht mehr bewegen.

s: daddy-longlegs, harvestman, water strider, cranefly, etc. (any long-legged arachnid or insect)

s: already (happening rather early, continuing rather long)
Es ist erst 11 Uhr und schon über 30 Grad im Schatten.
It’s only 11 a.m. and already more than 30 degrees (°C) in the shade.
Er ist schon seit drei Wochen krank.
He’s been sick for three weeks already.
previously, before (at some time in the past; but not: before a certain event)
Ich erinnere mich, dass wir solche Fälle schon hatten.
I remember that we had such cases before.
expresses that an action has been completed; already (but more frequent); yet (in questions)
Wir sind spät dran, aber diesen Stapel haben wir immerhin schon bearbeitet.
We’re running late, but at least we’ve (already) finished this pile.
Hast du dir schon die Zähne geputzt?
Have you brushed your teeth yet?
expresses a weighing of arguments, contrast between two statements, partial agreement, concession; admittedly; sure(ly); definitely; indeed
Man sollte Kinder nicht bestrafen. — Man sollte Kinder schon bestrafen, nur eben sinnvoll.
One shouldn’t punish children. — One should definitely punish children, but wisely.
Niedrige Steuern heben den Konsum. — Das ist schon richtig, aber...
Low taxes increase consumption. — That is admittedly true, but...
Used to add positive emphasis to a verb (which is frequently omitted), often when something else is negated. Compare si/sí/sì/sim in the Romance languages and wel in Dutch and Afrikaans.
Ich rauche nicht, aber du schon.
I don't smoke, but you do.
Mach die Glocke bei mir aus, wenn du weniger am Handy sein willst, aber abonnieren kannst du mich schon.
Turn off the bell on my channel if you want to spend less time on your phone, but you can still subscribe to me.

s: Er hat seiner Frau nie Schaden zugefügt.
He has never done any harm to his wife.
He must be out of his mind.
Schaden.et: From Middle High German schade, from Old High German skado, from Proto-West Germanic *skaþō, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô. Compare Dutch schade, Low German Schaden, Schaad, English scathe, Danish skade, Swedish skada.

s: disgrace, infamy, dishonour (state or result considered highly disreputable for whoever is responsible)
Schande.et: From Middle High German schande, from Old High German scanta, from Proto-West Germanic *skandu, from Proto-Germanic *skandō (“shame, disgrace”). Cognate with Yiddish שאַנדע (shande), English shand, Dutch schande.

s: sharp; able to cut (of a knife, edge)
sharp; tight (of a turn on a route)
sharp; severe; harsh (of criticism, attacks, glances)
keen on; excited for; strongly looking forward to
live; hot (of a bomb, firearm, ammunition)
scharf.et: From Middle High German scharpf, from Old High German scarf, from Proto-West Germanic *skarp, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Compare Low German scharp, Dutch scherp, English sharp, Danish skarp.

s: a large, unwieldy car (e.g. an SUV)
boiler (metal container for boiling water in some old stoves and ovens)
Schiff.et:
From Middle High German schif, from Old High German skif (“ship, barrel, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“ship, hollow object”). The sense “nave” is a semantic loan from Latin nāvis.
Cognate with Low German Schipp, West Fr…

s: Schiff: a surname originating as an occupation The occupational surname taken up by mariners and boatmen.
Schiff.et:
From Middle High German schif, from Old High German skif (“ship, barrel, vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“ship, hollow object”). The sense “nave” is a semantic loan from Latin nāvis.
Cognate with Low German Schipp, West Fr…

Schnur.et: From Middle High German snuor, from Old High German snuor, from Proto-Germanic *snōrō. Cognate with Dutch snoer. Also related to English snare.
From Middle High German snur, from Old High German snur, from Proto-West Germanic *snuʀu (“daughter-in-law”).

s: straightway, straight, directly (going somewhere immediately and by the shortest way possible)
a woman wearing a veil, usually an Islamic niqab

Schleier.et:
From Middle High German sleier, sleiger, sloiger, slogier. Of uncertain ultimate origin, but most likely borrowed; perhaps related to Latin stragulus (“covering”).
Compare Middle Low German sleyer, sloier, sloiger, Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyr…

s: any insect of the order Lepidoptera, i.e. a butterfly or moth
Schmetterling.et: Attested ca. 1500, standard since the 18th century. From an East Central German dialect word, equivalent to Schmetten (“cream”) + -ling, due to an old belief that butterflies eat milk products or, in a more ornamented form, that witches transform themselves in…

Schmetten.et: Borrowed from Czech smetana or Polish śmietana. Compare Schmand.

s: a butterfly fish of the cichlid family Pantodontidae
a butterflyfish of the family Chaetodontidae
any plant of the Faboideae subfamily.
Schmetterlingsblütler.et:
From Schmetterlingsblüte + -ler.
From the form of the flowers, resembling a butterfly.

Schale.et: From Middle High German schale, from Old High German scala, from Proto-West Germanic *skalu, from Proto-Germanic *skalō. Cognate with Dutch schaal (“shell”) and English shale. Also related with Dutch schil, English shell.

s: Er trug ihr gleichsam die volle Schale seines Zornes hin, besorgt, etwas davon zu verschütten und mit dem Zorne zugleich Einbuße an der Energie zu erleiden, deren er bei der Auseinandersetzung mit seiner Frau bedurfte.
Schale.et: From Middle High German schāle, from Old High German scāla, from Proto-Germanic *skēlō, related to *skaljō (“husk, shell”). Cognate with Dutch schaal (“bowl”).

s: to peel; to pare; to husk; to skin

schofel.et: Borrowed from Yiddish שפֿל (shofl, “shabby”), which is from Hebrew שָׁפָל (šāfāl).

schmackhaft.et: Inherited from Middle High German smachaft, equivalent to (Ge)schmack + -haft

schwach.et: From Middle High German swach, from Old High German *swah, from Proto-West Germanic *swak. Cognate with Dutch zwak, Scots swack, also English dialectal swack.

s: A coalition consisting of the Christian Democratic Union, Free Democratic Party, and the Greens.
Die FDP schließt in Baden-Württemberg ein Bündnis mit Grünen und SPD aus. Eine „Schwampel“ mit einem CDU-Ministerpräsidenten lehnt die SPD ab.
Schwampel.et: Blend of schwarz (“black”) + Ampel(koalition) (“coalition of SPD, FDP, and the Greens”); black is the party color of the CDU.

s: Was will der Schwanz von mir?
What does this prick want from me?
Schwanz.et: From Middle High German swanz, from swanzen (“to swing”), derived from swanken, whence modern German schwanken (“to wobble”). Compare also Middle Low German swansen, swensen (“to skip, dance, strut, twirl”). Cognate of Yiddish שוואַנץ (shvants).

s: dovetail (type of joint where adjoining boards are fastened by interlocking fan-shaped cutouts)
swallow, martin (small, migratory bird of the Hirundinidae family)
Schwalbe.et: From Middle High German swalwe, from Old High German swalwa, from Proto-West Germanic *swalwā. Cognate with Middle Dutch swaluwe (modern Dutch zwaluw), Old Saxon swala, Old English swealwe (modern English swallow), Old Norse svala (Danish svale, Swedish svala)…

schal.et: From (late and northern) Middle High German schal (“tasteless, turbid”), borrowed from Middle Low German schal, from Proto-Germanic *skal-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to dry out”). Compare Swedish skäll (“thin, weak, bleak”), Old English sċe…

s: Was steht dahinten auf dem Schild?
What does that sign say over there?
label, tag (piece of paper etc. on a product)
Du musst noch das Schild an deinem neuen Hemd abschneiden.
You still have to cut off the label from your new shirt.
Schild.et: From Middle High German schilt m (“shield”) (genitive schiltes or schildes), from Old High German skilt, from Proto-West Germanic *skeldu, from Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keyt- (“shield, cover”). Cognate with Dutch schild,…

Medieval shields were often quite heavy.
Die Stasi begriff sich als Schild und Schwert der Partei.
The Stasi considered itself the Party’s shield and sword.

Schildkröte.et:
By surface analysis, compound of Schild (“shield”) + Kröte (“toad”).
Inherited from Middle High German (die/ein) schiltkräd (plural: schiltkräden; 2nd half of the 15th century), (ain) schiltkroten (ca. 1350).

s: Und indem sie auf Ljewin statt der ausdrücklichen Frage, ob er rauchen wolle, einen fragenden Blick richtete, zog sie ein Zigarettenkästchen aus Schildpatt zu sich heran und nahm sich eine Pajilla heraus.
Schildpatt.et: Middle Low German schildepadde, compare Dutch schildpad (“tortoise”).

s: to depict (with words), to narrate, tell vividly
Der Autor schildert die Erlebnisse seines Helden in bunten Farben.
The author depicts his hero’s adventures in vivid colours.
to depict (by illustration), to paint, draw

Scheitel.et:

to get a splinter into one's finger by accident
Schiefer.et: From Middle High German schiver, from Old High German skivaro. Related with Scheibe and scheiden.

Schnaps.et: From German Low German Snapps, originally “a sip (of liquor)”. Related to schnappen.

s: flat piece or surface: slice (e.g. of bread)
flat piece or surface: pane (of glass)

s: Am Nachmittag begannen sie, das Heu in Schober zu setzen.
Schober.et: From Middle High German schober, from Old High German scobar, itself from the Proto-Germanic stem *skup- (“barn, shed”), from which also Schopf, Schuppen and English shop.

s: narrow, slender (not wide, comparatively long), small
schmal.et: From Middle High German smal, from Old High German smal, from Proto-Germanic *smalaz. Cognate with Dutch smal, Low German small, English small.

Schutzstaffel.et: From Schutz + Staffel, literally “protection squadron, defence corps”.

s: shower (instance of something bursting forth like a rainshower)
Schauer.et: From Middle High German schūr, from Old High German scūr, from Proto-West Germanic *skūr, from Proto-Germanic *skūrō. Cognate with Dutch schoer, English shower, Swedish skur.

s: roof or open shed for taking shelter
Schauer.et: From Middle High German schūr, from Old High German scūr, northern variant of skiura, whence Scheuer (“shed, barn”).

s: inspector, one who inspects (e.g. the quality of goods)
Schauer.et: From Middle High German schouwære, from Old High German schouwāri. Equivalent to schauen + -er.

s: dock worker who loads and unloads ships, lumper
Schauer.et: 19th century, from Low German Schauer, from Dutch sjouwer, derived from sjouwen, from West Frisian sjouwe.

s: sleep (dried mucus in the corner of the eyes)
Schlaf.et:
From earlier Slaf, from Middle High German slāf, from Old High German slāf, from Proto-West Germanic *slāp.
Cognate with Hunsrik Schlof, Luxembourgish Schlof, Low German Slaap, Dutch slaap, and English sleep.

s: »Heute sind offiziell die ersten drei Geparde eingetroffen«, sagte Verteidigungsminister Olexij Resnikow am Montag im ukrainischen Fernsehen. Dazu seien auch mehrere Zehntausend Schuss übergeben worden.
Und ich passte immer auf, dass ich immer genug H für den Schuss am nächsten Morgen aufbewahrte.
And I always made sure I always saved enough H for next morning's shot.
coke with a dash of rum
Schuss.et:
From Middle High German schuȥ, from Old High German scuȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *skuti; whence English shoot and skeet.
Cognate with Dutch scheut, Old English scyte, Icelandic skutur. Related to schießen and Schoss.

s:
Die regelmäßige Verjährungsfrist beginnt, soweit nicht ein anderer Verjährungsbeginn bestimmt ist, mit dem Schluss des Jahres, in dem
1. der Anspruch entstanden ist und

The regular timeframe for liberative prescription, if no other term is stated, begins with the conclusion of the year in which
1. the claim has arisen and
2. the owner of the claim has gained knowledge or with gross negligence not gained knowledge of the circumstances having given rise to the claim as well as of the person of the debtor.
Schluss.et: From late Middle High German sluz, ultimately from the root of schließen (“to close, shut”). Compare Dutch slot. Related to English slot.

Schutz.et: From Middle High German schuz. See the verb schützen (“to defend”).

Schütze.et: From Middle High German schütze, from Old High German scuzzo, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, *skuttijaną (“to bar, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *skuttą, *skuttjō (“bar, bolt, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”). Compare Engl…

Starting tomorrow/from tomorrow onwards we will have school again.

Schule.et: From Middle High German schuole, from Old High German scuola.

As long as the German Reich exists, the screw will be turned to the right.
screw: a propeller advancing by helical movement
screw: the simple machine called screw
screw: the abstracted form things may acquire called helix
screw: a spiral movement, a spin around the longitudinal axis
screw: a spiral movement around the longitudinal axis formalized in athletics
Schraube.et: From Middle High German schrūbe. The earlier developments seem not to be quite clear; see screw for more.

s: scraper, flat instrument with a handle used for scraping
Schabe.et:
From Middle High German schabe (“scraper, chaff, moulding; moth, cockroach”), from Old High German scaba (“scraper, plane”), from Proto-Germanic *skabō (“scraper”).
Cognate with Dutch schaaf (“plane”). Also related to German Low German Schabbe (“mange, scabies…

Schacht.et: Borrowed from Middle Low German schacht, from Old Saxon skaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schaft.

s: upper (of a shoe), leg (of a boot)
Schaft.et: From Middle High German schaft, from Old High German skaft, scaft, from Proto-West Germanic *skaft. Doublet of Schacht.

s: a small, usually square box, package or case
Schachtel.et: 15th century, from Italian scatola, with metathesis from Latin castulum, itself a diminutive of Lombardic Old High German kasto. Hence a doublet of inherited Kasten as well as the later borrowing Schatulle. The -ch- is due to a Bavarian consonantal development…

I see a thousand eyes, and they're closed / Knock on a thousand doors and none are open / I drink and drink till my head is pounding
headache, particularly one due to excessive drinking

I'm not back, I was never away, your girlfriend is giving me head
Ich muss große Träume leben, krieg' von Rotlichtbräuten Schädel
Schädel.et: From Middle High German schedel (“skull”). Further origin uncertain. Borrowing from Middle Low German schêdel (“top of the head, head, skull”), cognate with German Scheitel (“top of the head, parting of the hair”), suggests itself, but is not embraced in most …

s: a surname originating as an occupation, equivalent to English Shepherd
Schäfer.et: From Middle High German schæfære, from late Old High German scāphāre. Equivalent to Schaf (“sheep”) + -er. Compare Dutch schaper, scheper.

any swinging construction, including seesaws and similar devices

s: a resonating sound, one that is either very loud or reverberant
Schall.et:
From Middle High German schal, from Old High German scal, from Proto-West Germanic *skellan, from Proto-Germanic *skellaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”).

Scham.et: From Middle High German schame, from Old High German scama, from Proto-West Germanic *skamu, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European [Term?]. Compare Dutch schaamte, English shame, Danish skam.

Schar.et: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German scara (“troop”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō. Cognate with English share, Swedish skara.
From Middle High German schar, from Old High German scaro. Cognate with German scheren (“to shear”), German Schere (“shear, scissors”), English share (“plowshare”), English shear.

s: to give as a present, to gift
Ich schenke meiner Tochter ein Kätzchen zum Geburtstag.
I’m giving my daughter a kitten for her birthday.
Joseph hätte sich die beschwerliche weite Reise gern geschenkt, doch er wagte es nicht, ungehorsam zu sein.
Joseph would have gladly spared himself the long, onerous journey, but he didn't dare to be disobedient.
to pour from a vessel, to serve
Sie schenkte den Wein in zwei Gläser.
She poured the wine in two glasses.

Why are you looking so angry?

Keine Sorge, ich schau, dass du nicht ins Gefängnis kommst.
Don't worry, I'll see to it that you don't go to jail.

Schicht.et: From northern Middle High German schiht, from Middle Low German schicht, schichte, derived from the verb schichten (whence German schichten). Cognate with Dutch schicht, English shift.

Entfernen Sie dieses Fahrzeug von der Schiene.
Remove this vehicle from the rail.

They want to use the money to repair tracks, bridges and train stations.
a staff on which something moves: rack
a staff or long construction that holds things together: orthotics; splint
a staff or long construction that holds things together: frame; skid
Schiene.et: Inherited from Middle High German schine, from Old High German skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu. Cognate with Dutch scheen, English shin.

Schilf.et: From Middle High German schilf, from Old High German sciluf, from Proto-West Germanic *skilp, *skilup (“reed, rush”).

s: a paddle used in the game of hornussen
Schindel.et: From Middle High German schindel, from Old High German scintula, from Proto-West Germanic *skindulā (“roof-shingle”).

screen (movable protective cover): bill, peak (of a cap)
Schirm.et:
From Middle High German schirm, scherm, from Old High German skerm, skirm (“screen”), from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi (“fur, pelt, covering, screen”).
More at screen. Compare scrim.

Schlacht.et: From Middle High German slaht, from Old High German slahta, ultimately from the root of schlagen (“to strike, hit”). Compare Danish slag (“battle, strike”). Cognate of English slaughter.

Schlacke.et: From Middle Low German slagge (“slag”, older “splinter of hammered iron”, 14th c.), from slān (“to hit, strike”), the cognate of German schlagen. Compare Dutch slak, English slag, both also from Middle Low German.

Schlacke.et: Alteration of Schalke based on etymology 1 above, suggested by the club’s origins in, and continued association with, coal mining.

From Middle High German slaf, from Old High German slaf, from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”).

The bread went bad and green fungi grew on it.

I always get sick from too many sweets.

Schlauch.et: From Middle High German slūch (“waterskin, snakeskin, slough”). Immediately cognate with Old Saxon slūk, also related with English slough. From the same root as schlüpfen (“to hatch, slip”).

Schleim.et: From Middle High German slīm, from Old High German slīm, from Proto-Germanic *slīmą. Cognate with Dutch slijm, English slime.

s: throat, pharynx (interior of the front of the neck)
maw (open mouth of a dangerous creature)
Schlund.et: From Middle High German and Old High German slunt, from the root of schlingen (“to swallow, gulp”).

english (spin imparted on a billiard ball by hitting it on the side)
Schmalz.et: From Middle High German smalz, from Old High German smalz, from Proto-West Germanic *smalt (“(molten) fat, lard”), an ablaut derivative of *smeltaną. Doublet of Emaille. The figurative sense in part as a backformation from schmalzig.

s: a surname — famously held by: Valentin Schmalz (1572–1622), German Socinian theologian
Schmalz.et: Attested in the 13th century in Schleswig-Holstein, thought to derive from Middle Low German smal (“small”), from Proto-Germanic *smalaz. Compare the English surname Small, Smalls.

Schmied.et: From Middle High German smit, from Old High German smid, from Proto-West Germanic *smiþ, from Proto-Germanic *smiþaz.

s: a surname originating as an occupation, variant of Schmidt and Schmitt
Schmied.et: From Middle High German smit, from Old High German smid, from Proto-West Germanic *smiþ, from Proto-Germanic *smiþaz.

s: anything that fastens and secures the position of something, clasp, frequently

Vielleicht hat man schon seit Jahrhunderten einen säuerlichen Geschmack empfunden, wenn man eine silberne Schnalle so in den Mund nahm, daß der Rand derselben die obere, der Dorn die untere Zungenfläche berührte.
Maybe for centuries already one has felt a sourish taste when one put a silver clasp in the mouth in such a manner that the rim of it touched the upper, the spine the lower tongue surface.
clasp on vestments, item fastened to a garment not without decorative functions, like or particularly a buckle of a belt
vulva of a wolf or fox
woman: baggage, member of the other sex

s: cutlet, scallop, escalope (slice of filet meat)
Schnitzel.et: From Schnitz (“cut-off piece”) + -el. Pertaining to schneiden (“to cut”). The culinary sense spread from Austria and was therefore adopted in the regional neuter gender.

Schnorchel.et: Early 20th century, deverbal from Low German schnorgeln, snörgeln (“to snore, snuffle”, attested 19th century). So called because of the stertorous sound. Related to schnarchen (“to snore”). Doublet of obsolete Schnörchel (“a certain disease of pigeons”).

Das Huhn im schnellen Fluge, / die Schnepf im Zickzackzuge / treff ich mit Sicherheit
The fowl in its quick dash / The snipe in zigzags / With a sure hand I squash
Schnepfe.et: From Middle High German snepfe, from Old High German snepfa, from the root of Schnabel (“beak, pecker”). Related to Icelandic mýrisnípa.

Schnupfen.et: From Middle High German snupfen, an intensive formation related to schnauben (“to snort”) (DWDS).

s: a flat, brittle piece of something, chiefly of earth (a clod) or ice (a floe)
Scholle.et: From Middle High German scholle m or f, from Old High German scollo m, scolla f. The feminine gender is chiefly Central and Low German. Cognate with Dutch schol, Middle Low German scholle.
16th century, from Middle Low German scholle. Probably from figurative use of etymology 1.

s: to grab someone by the hair
crown (feathers sticking up at the back of a bird's head)
the long hair on a horse's forehead

Cognate with Middle Low German schōde, Old Norse skauð, and perhaps the first element in Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍀…

s: gate (barrier that can be pulled or moved up to allow passage)
a level crossing with such a gate
some other kind of barrier or limit
Schranke.et: From Middle High German schranke, related to Old High German firskrenken (“to prevent”), German schränken (“to put or pile things crosswise”), from Proto-Germanic *skrankaz (“barrier, grid”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”).

s: step, footstep (a single instance of walking)

Gebt Raum, ihr Völker, unsrem Schritt.
Wir sind die letzten Goten.
Wir tragen keine Krone mit,

Make way, ye peoples, before our footstep.
We are the last of the Goths,
We carry no crown with us,
We carry a corpse.
crotch (the area between the human legs close to the genitals or comprising them)

any imaginary measure that is likened in its partitioning to the distance traveled by a leg moving forward in its single footsteps
Er war uns einige Schritte voraus.
He was a few steps ahead of us.
step, move, stage (the part of a measure in the sense of an action one takes)
Um dieses Ziel zu erreichen, sind folgende Schritte durchzuführen:
To reach this end, the following steps need to be performed:

Schrot.et: From Middle High German schrōt, from Old High German scrōt, from Proto-Germanic *skraudō.

Schrott.et: From Ripuarian and Low Franconian Schrott (“scrap”), which is the same word as German Schrot (“groats”). The regional form is not, however, derived from Middle High German schrōt, but from a variant Middle High German schrāt, Middle Dutch *scraet (compare atte…

Schuft.et: According to Kluge, borrowed from Middle Low German schūvūt (“eagle owl”) (itself onomatopoeic in origin). The word may have been applied to criminals because, like the bird, they shy away from the light of day.

s: scale (keratin pieces covering the skin of certain animals)
piece of dandruff; and in the plural: dandruff
Schuppe.et:
From Middle High German schuope, schuoppe, schuppe, from Old High German scuobba, scuopa, from earlier *skōbba, ultimately from the root of schaben (“to scrape”).
Cognate with Middle Low German schōpe, schōve, schubbe. One of the rare words with a long vowel f…

Schuppen.et: A nominal formation related to Schopf (“tuft, crown (of feathers)”), as they were originally covered with bundles of straw. Cognate with dialectal English shippon (“cow-shed”),, also cognate with English shop.

s: shoemaker, cobbler (of male or unspecified sex)
Schuster.et: From Middle High German schuochsūtære, from Old High German *skuohsūteri, from Proto-West Germanic *skōhasūtārī (“shoemaker”).

s: a surname originating as an occupation
Schuster.et: From Middle High German schuochsūtære, from Old High German *skuohsūteri, from Proto-West Germanic *skōhasūtārī (“shoemaker”).

Schutt.et: From Late Middle High German schut.

s: Ist dieser Schwager der Mann Ihrer Schwester oder der Bruder Ihrer Frau?
Is this brother-in-law your sister’s husband or your wife’s brother?
in-law; a fairly distant relative by marriage
Das ist irgendein entfernter Schwager von mir.
He’s some distant in-law of mine.
Schwager.et: From Middle High German swāger, from Old High German swāger, swāgur, from Proto-West Germanic *swāgr, from Proto-Germanic *swēgraz (“husband's brother”), from Proto-Indo-European *swēḱurós (“brother-in-law”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“husban…

Schwall.et: From Middle High German swal, from the root of schwellen (“to swell”).

Schwamm.et: From Middle High German swamme, swam, swamp, from Old High German swamp, from Proto-West Germanic *swamm, from Proto-Germanic *swambaz, *swammaz. See also Old English swamm.

Schwan.et:
From Middle High German swan, from Old High German swan, from Proto-West Germanic *swan, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”), from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”).
Compare Low German Swaan, Dutch zwaan, English swan, Swedish svan.

s: Sie ist schwanger von ihrem Mann Peter mit ihrem dritten Kind.
She is pregnant from her husband Peter with her third child.
schwanger.et: From Middle High German swanger, from Old High German swangar, from Proto-West Germanic *swangr (“heavy”), further origin unknown. Cognate with Old English swangor, Dutch zwanger (“pregnant”), Yiddish שוואַנגער (shvanger, “pregnant”), and Norwegian Bokmål svan…

s: swarm of insects; flock of birds; school of fish
Dazu zirpten unzählige Zikaden, schillernde Libellen schossen surrend durch die Luft, […], Mücken summten in Schwärmen, […]
In addition countless cicadas chirped, iridescent dragonflies shot buzzingly through the air, […], mosquitoes hummed in swarms, […]
crush; beloved; object of one’s (unfulfilled) love
Schwarm.et:
From Middle High German swarm, from Old High German swarm, from Proto-Germanic *swarmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to buzz, hum”).
Compare Dutch zwerm, English swarm, Danish sværm. The sense “crush” is a backformation from the verb schwärmen; see there…

Schwindel.et: From Middle High German [Term?]. Cognate with Hunsrik Schwinnel.

s: Mit einem Schwung warf er alle Akten vom Tisch.
In one sweep he threw all the files off the desk.
a quantity so swept, (hence colloquial) any large amount
Sie knallte mir einen Schwung Akten auf den Tisch.
She banged a pile of files onto my desk.
momentum, speed, force (intensity of a specific movement)
Du musst mit mehr Schwung über die Rampe fahren, wenn du weiter springen willst.
You need to go over the ramp with more speed if you want to jump further.
Er soll die flaue Wirtschaft wieder in Schwung bringen.
His job is to stir the sagging economy.
Die Show wirkt altbacken, sie braucht wieder mehr Schwung.
The show feels stodgy, it needs to get some pep back.
Schwung.et: From Middle High German swunc, ablaut derivation from swingen, modern schwingen (“to swing”). Originally infrequent, but in general use since the 18th century.

s: to swing (to move back and forth)
She is swinging on a swing.
to swing (to move something using a swinging motion)
Das grundlegende Problem aller optischen Mikroskope ist das Licht: Es schwingt, je nach Farbe, mit einer Wellenlänge von einigen hundert Nanometern.
The fundamental problem of all optical microscopes is the light: it oscillates, depending on the color, with a wavelength of a few hundred nanometers.
to propagate (somewhere) as sound, to move throughout (an area) resounding
der Klang der Glocken schwang durch die Stadt
the sound of the bells resounded throughout the city
to clean (hemp or flax) of wood residues

schwingen.et: From Middle High German swingen, from Old High German swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą. Cognate with Low German swingen, English swing. Doublet of swingen.

Schwur.et: From Middle High German swuor, from Old High German swuor, from Proto-Germanic *swōraz (“oath”), from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”). Compare English swear and Vilamovian śwür.

Schwiegermutter.et: Expanded from earlier Schwieger (“mother-in-law”), from Old High German swigar, from Proto-Germanic *swegrō, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱruh₂- (“woman's mother-in-law”) (compare *swéḱuros (“woman's father-in-law”)). By surface analysis, schwieger- + Mutter.

s: Freunde exotischer Gerichte verbrennen sich mitunter gehörig den Mund, weil sie die Schärfe falsch einschätzen.
Friends of exotic dishes now and then awfully burn their mouth, because they misjudge the spiciness.
Die katholische Kirche will ihre Missbrauchsopfer finanziell nicht durch eine pauschale Summe entschädigen, sondern individuell je nach Schwere des Falls.
The Catholic Church wants to financially compensate their abuse victims not with a lump sum, but individually according to the severity of the case.
Schwere.et: Middle High German swære, from Old High German swārī, from Proto-West Germanic *swārī, from Proto-Germanic *swērį̄; equivalent to schwer + -e. Cognate with British English sweer.

s: to issue, run, post an advertisement
to be on the ball (to be quick to understand and react to something sudden and/or unexpected)

schwellen.et: From Middle High German swëllen, from Old High German *swellen (only attested in biswellen), from Proto-Germanic *swallijaną, causative verb of *swellaną.

schmutzig.et: From Schmutz + -ig, whence also dialectal Dutch smotsig. Compare also English smutty.

s: chocolate (food made from ground roasted cocoa beans)
Schokolade.et: Borrowed from Dutch chocolade, from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.

s: shoe tree (to hold or stretch a shoe)
a common surname originating as an occupation, equivalent to English Smith
speed, velocity, rapidness, quickness (state/degree of moving or proceeding fast)
Die Schnelligkeit der Lieferung hat mich überrascht.
The quickness of the delivery surprised me.
speed, the ability to move, especially run, fast
Er muss noch an seiner Schnelligkeit arbeiten.
He has to work on his top speed.
Schnelligkeit.et: From Middle High German snellecheit, an extended form of Middle and Old High German snelheit. Equivalent to schnell + -igkeit. The simpler form Schnellheit is now substandard, but may still be heard (chiefly as an ad-hoc formation); compare Dutch snelheid.

Scheherazade.et:
Borrowed from Russian Шехераза́да (Šexerazáda), from Persian شهرازاد (šahrâzâd), alternative form of شهرزاد (šahrzâd, literally “child of the city”), from شهر (šahr, “city”) + ـزاد (-zâd, “child of”).
The noun is a reference to the fictional character.

s: a female storyteller or narrator of fairy tales
Scheherazade.et:
Borrowed from Russian Шехераза́да (Šexerazáda), from Persian شهرازاد (šahrâzâd), alternative form of شهرزاد (šahrzâd, literally “child of the city”), from شهر (šahr, “city”) + ـزاد (-zâd, “child of”).
The noun is a reference to the fictional character.

Schaltjahr.et: From Middle High German schaltjār, from Old High German scaltjār, from scaltan (“to push forward”).

Scharlatan.et: Borrowed from French charlatan, from Italian ciarlatano.

s: the working dog of a swine-herd

Schrei.et: From Middle High German schrei, schrē, from Old High German screi. First attested in the 9th century. Cognate with Hunsrik Schreu. Ultimately from the root of schreien (“to shout, cry out”).

Schock.et: Chiefly a borrowing (since 18th century), partly from French choc, partly from English shock, both derived from Old French choquer, from Frankish *skokkōn. There was also an uncommon native cognate, from Middle High German schoc (“wind gust”, rarely also “shoc…

s: three score (a unitless measure indicating sixty of anything)
one score; two score (a unitless measure indicating twenty or forty of anything)
a heap, a bunch (a large, indefinite number)
Schock.et: Compare Dutch schok, Danish skok, Swedish skock, Norwegian skok.

s: a surname originating as an occupation

Schornstein.et: From Middle High German schor(n)stein, Old High German scorrenstein. The first element is from schore (“support”), related to the root of scheren (“to cut”); the second element is from Stein (“stone”).

Schlüsselbein.et: 17th century, from Schlüssel (“key”) + Bein (“bone”), after New Latin clāvicula (literally “little key”). Compare Dutch sleutelbeen, Swedish nyckelben, Czech klíční kost, etc., some of which may be loan translations of the German.

Schimpanse.et: From a Bantu language, probably via French chimpanzé.

s: Das Schnitzwerk seines Gesimses stellte kleine, pausbäckige Engelchen dar, die zwischen allerhand Schnörkeln, wie in einem Irrgarten gefangen saßen.
The carving of its moulding depicted small, chubby-faced little angels, which sat between all sorts of embellishments, like trapped in a maze.

Schleife.et: From Middle High German sleife, from Old High German sleifa, from sleifen, whence modern schleifen (“to drag”).

to swarm; to fly in swarms or flocks

to gush; to rave about; to be enthusiastic about

schläfrig.et: From Middle High German slæferic, slāferic, from Old High German slāfrag, slāferag. By surface analysis, Schläfer (“sleeper”) + -ig.

scheußlich.et: From Middle High German schiuzlîch, reshaped under the influence of Scheusal; see scheuen for more.

s: spongy (having the structure of a sponge)
Ich hatte in meinem Leben vorher nie etwas Widerlicheres gesehen, als diesen mageren, bebrillten, greisenhaften, kichernden Mann und seine schwammige, übel aufgeputzte Frau.

Schraubstock.et: 16th century, from schrauben (“to screw”) + Stock (literally “stick, trunk”). The latter word here probably continues the use of Middle High German stoc for a kind of wooden block used to shackle prisoners. Compare also French étau.

Schreibmaschine.et: From schreiben (“write”) + Maschine (“machine”). Cognate with Hunsrik Schreibmaschin, Plautdietsch Schriewmaschien.

Schnurrbart.et: A borrowing from German Low German Snurrbaart, equivalent to schnurren (“to purr”) + Bart (“beard”), thus the "purring beard", perhaps owing to its tendency to rustle when its owner speaks or "purrs", or perhaps due to its resemblance to the whiskers of a purr…

s: to purr (produce a vibrating, whirring sound, especially when satisfied)
Unsere Katze schnurrt immer, wenn sie merkt, dass ihr Fressen vorbereitet wird.
Our cat always purrs when she notices that her meal is being prepared.
to produce a “healthy” sound that indicates good function

to slaughter (kill livestock; kill people brutally)

Schurke.et: Derived from Middle High German schurgen, schürgen (“to shove, push, egg on”) in the 16th century, from Old High German scurgen. This verb is related to (but probably not the direct ancestor of) modern schüren (“to stir, stoke up”); compare Old High German fiu…

Criminals don't necessarily win by spying on individuals. Instead, they take advantage of the mass distribution of malware.

Schlumpf.et: Alteration of French schtroumpf, itself probably from German Strumpf (“stocking”). Whether the form was coined at random by the German translator or whether it was influenced by the surname below or perhaps by some other word, appears to be unknown.

schrecklich.et: Schreck + -lich; from Late Middle High German [Term?].

Schreck.et:
From Middle High German schrecke, from Old High German screcko, formed from the noun screckōn (“to jump around, surge, flash out, rebound”), from where is also derived schrecken (“to frighten”), which see for further.
Compare Dutch schrik.

s: Black Forest (a mountainous region in southwestern Germany)

s: to remove ballast from railway tracks to sabotage operations, especially nuclear waste movements.
Die Kampagne „Castor schottern" spricht von fast 1 000 verletzten Demonstranten, die meisten von ihnen hätten Augenverletzungen erlitten.
The "Sabotage Nuclear Waste Flasks" campaign spoke of nearly 1,000 injured protestors, most of whom would have suffered eye injuries.
Streckenschutz, um die Bahngleise zu bewachen, um ein Schottern oder Blockieren zu vermeiden oder ein Zerstören von Signal- und Gleisanlagen zu unterbinden.
Line protection to watch the railway tracks, in order to avoid a ballast removal or blockage or to prevent the destruction of signal and track equipment.

Schotte.et: From Middle High German Schotte, Schote. Probably from Old English Sċott, perhaps borrowed through Middle Dutch Scotte. In any case, ultimately from Latin Scōtus.

Middle High German -schaft, from Old High German -skaft, -skaf, from Proto-West Germanic *-skapi.
Cognate with Dutch -schap, Swedish -skap, English -ship, Danish -skab, West Frisian -skip. Final -t possibly from Proto-Germanic *-þiz, as seen in *gaskaftiz.

Am Wald, jenseits der Schonung, standen drei Rehe.
Three roe deer were standing by the woods, beyond the copse of young trees.
defeat, flop, disadvantageous outcome (in a game, election, contest, battle etc.)
Einen AfD-Bürgermeister gibt es in Nordrhein-Westfalen zum Glück weiter nicht. Die drei Stichwahl-Kandidaten in Gelsenkirchen, Duisburg und Hagen kassierten klare Schlappen.

slide, slipper (one of a pair of footwear open in the back, a shoe from which the back has been cut off)

Schwarzpulver.et: From schwarz (“black”) + Pulver (“powder”). A popular folk etymology claims the legendary alchemist and alleged inventor Berthold Schwarz as origin.

something that has been washed ashore: flood, glut (sudden abundance of something)
an area of shallow water where people or, more often, animals bathe themselves
part of a beer hall or large pub, originally that reserved for the lower classes, now one where people either stand or otherwise sit in large numbers at simple tables
Schwemme.et: From Middle High German swemme, deverbal from swemmen, whence modern schwemmen (“to sweep, to wash ashore”), which see for more. The sense “part of a beer hall” derives via “simple tavern” (16th c.) from the formerly current expression die Zunge in die Schwemm…

Er war schwermütig geworden, konnte nicht, oder nicht recht arbeiten und hatte Sorge um die Erhaltung seiner Existenz, also melancholische Depression mit Arbeitshemmung und (berechtigter) Lebenssorge.
He had become melancholic, could not work, or not well, and had worries about sustaining his existence, thus a melancholic depression with work block and (justified) worries about life.
to hurt, to ache (to cause physical/bodily pain, often of parts of one's own body)
Der Wind schnitt ihm ins Gesicht, die Ohren schmerzten ihn, und die Nase fühlte sich auf dem Handrücken, mit dem er darüberwischte, kalt und feucht an.
The wind cut his face, his ears hurt, and as he wiped across his nose with the back of his hand, it felt cold and wet.
Aha. Dann war der Zahn also empfindlich geworden und schmerzte vorher also schon von ganz alleine, oder?
I see. Then the tooth had turned sensitive and been aching all on its own previous to that, right?

Suddenly my father came out; he had been making a rumpus in the mill since daybreak, and his nightcap sat awry on his head.
Köhlers Fazit: „Die Bürger sind keine Schlafmützen, sie wollen sich kümmern.“
Vierzig mal 365 Tage und dazu noch die Schalttage waren verstrichen, seit Dorothee unter den Apfelbäumen Burkahnens über ihr Leben entschieden hatte.
Forty times 365 days and in addition the leap days had passed since Dorothee had decided her future life under the apple trees of Burkahnen.

Scharbockskraut.et: From Scharbock (“scurvy”) + Kraut (“helpful plant”), due to the richness in vitamins.

Once again there had been heated debates between animal rights activists and ones who consider bullfighting a cultural heritage of Spain worth protecting.
a type of freestyle wrestling practiced in Switzerland
Im Schwingen bewährte sich die Meisterschaft der Berner, im Steinstoßen siegten die Appenzeller […]
In wrestling, the mastery of the Bernese persevered, in stone putting, the Appenzellians were victorious […]
Schwingen.et:
Verbal noun, substantivation of schwingen.
The sense "Swiss wrestling" is attested from the 16th century, often in the phrase "Ringen und Schwingen".

s: "Aber soll denn jeder Schwachkopf, wenn er nur Geld hat, studiren dürfen?" Nein! keinem Schwächlinge dieser Art soll die Schranke geöffnet werden.
"But should every idiot who has money be allowed to study?" No! For no weakling of this kind the barrier should be opened.
"Hiob? Dieser Schwachkopf, dem Gott jede Menge Unheil schickte, um ihn auf die Probe zu stellen?"
"Job? That idiot to whom God sent a lot of harm in order to test him?"
Schwachkopf.et: schwach (“weak”) + Kopf (“head”). Compare with weakheaded, weakminded, Russian слабоу́мный (slaboúmnyj, “imbecile, weakminded”).

s: Der Autosalon in Moskau zählt zu den internationalen Schaubühnen für Fahrzeuginteressierte mit unbegrenzten Ansprüchen.
The motor show in Moscow is reckoned among the international stages for people interested in vehicles with unlimited demands.
Seit der rumänische Wirtschaftsboom vor zwei Jahren schlagartig mit der Finanzkrise zu Ende ging, ist die Arbeitslosigkeit im Land auf mehr als sieben Prozent gestiegen.
Since the Romanian economic boom abruptly came to an end with the financial crisis two years ago, the unemployment in te country rose to more than seven percent.

schweren.et: From Middle High German swæren, from Old High German swārēn, from Proto-West Germanic *swārēn, from Proto-Germanic *swērāną.

s:
O könnt' ich fliegen wie Tauben dahin,
weit hinweg vor dem Feinde zu fliehn!
In die Wüste eilt' ich dann fort,

Oh, if I could fly off like the doves,
flee far away from the foe!
Into the wilderness I would then hasten,
and find repose in a shadowy place.

Schmier.et: Borrowed from Yiddish שמירה (shmire), from Hebrew שמירה (šəmīrā, “guard”). Compare Schmiere stehen.

s: diagonal relationship (of elements in the periodic table)
generic term for center of mass and center of gravity
focus, emphasis, main point, center of gravity
spelling (specific way of writing a word)
Eines Tages kehrten wir sogar in eine Konditorei ein, und zum erstenmal im Leben durfte ich Schokolade mit Schlagobers genießen.

Schub.et: From Middle High German schub, schup, ultimately from the root of and a deverbal from schieben (“to shove”). Cognate to English shove.

Schubs.et: From Schupp (“push”) + -s (“intensive nominal ending”). Schupp (15th c.) is deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. See schu…

s: Die Weltseele scheint noch ein unerzogenes Mädchen mit ihren Bildungen aus Erdschollen zu spielen, sie hängt fast immer einen gewaltigen Geist und ein gewaltiges Schicksal einem schwachen Körper zum Schabernack an.

Sonst habe ich nichts wider ihn vorgenommen, noch vornehmen wollen. Der Knecht dachte nach. — Vor Schabernack brauche ich den Alten nicht zu bewahren, sondern nur vor Stehlen, Brennen und Viehschaden ; […]
Schabernack.et: From Middle High German schabirnack, from Middle Low German schavernak (14th c.). Further etymology unknown.

s: A furnace, specifically to smelt metals, a smelter

An old variant of schnauben (“to snort, to pant”), documented in Middle High German snūfen.
The fricative -f- (or -v-) instead of -b- is expected for Low German (compare Middle Low German snûven) as well as West Central German (compare Luxembourgish schnauwen)…

Schilling.et: From Middle High German schillinc, from Old High German skilling, from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz.

s: Schwarzerden, a municipality in the district of Bad Kreuznach in Germany
area where there is chernozem/black earth
Das Schöne ist, dass ich jetzt mehr Freizeit habe.
The nice thing is that I have more free time now.
the beauty [i.e. the beautiful woman] and the beast
beauty, the quality of being beautiful
Schöne.et: From Middle High German schœne, from Old High German scōnī, from Proto-Germanic *skaunį̄. Analysable as schön + -e.

s: the state of being without frills; straightforwardness
one of the seven days of creation
Wütend schmetterte er seine Tasche in die Ecke.
He furiously smashed his bag into a corner.
to yell (something) in a resounding voice, especially in a commanding or sharp tone
Der Feldwebel schmetterte seine Befehle über den Exerzierplatz.
The sergeant yelled his commands over the parade ground.
Er hatte viel zu viel getrunken und schmetterte derbe Sprüche durch den Saal.
He had had a lot too much to drink and yelled ribald remarks through the hall.
Sie lagen sich in den Armen und schmetterten die neuesten Karnevalsschlager.
They were all embracing each other, belting out the most recent carnival songs.
Die Fanfaren schmetterten durch die engen Gassen.
The fanfares were sounding through the narrow lanes.

Die armen Weiber sind doch übel dran: / Ein Hagestolz ist schwerlich zu bekehren.
